title: A Patiala Illustrator's Silent Ode to Indian Rooftops Wins London's Batsford Prize
excerpt: Anantjeet Kaur's wordless accordion book 'Terrace Tales' captures the life that unfolds on Indian chhat — kite fights, pickle-drying, late-night conversations — and just earned one of Britain's most prestigious illustration awards.
body:
If you grew up in India, you know the rooftop. Not the manicured terraces of architectural magazines, but the real thing — the chhat where your grandmother dried papad in summer, where kites battled during Makar Sankranti, where cousins slept on charpoys under an ink-blue sky because the power was out and the rooms were unbearable. The rooftop is where Indian domestic life breathes, and Anantjeet Kaur has turned it into art.

## The Book That Needs No Words

Kaur, a young illustrator from Patiala now pursuing an MA in Children's Book Illustration at Cambridge School of Art (Anglia Ruskin University), won the Book Illustration category at the 2026 Batsford Prize — one of Britain's most respected awards for emerging artists — for her accordion book *Terrace Tales: A Celebration of Indian Rooftops*.

The format is as distinctive as its subject. An accordion book unfolds horizontally, panel by panel, like a panoramic scroll. Kaur's version is entirely wordless: the narrative lives in the illustrations alone, each panel revealing a different rooftop scene that any Indian viewer will recognise instantly.

The Batsford Prize, now in its seventh year, awards £4,000 across four categories — applied art, fine art, architecture, and book illustration. This year's theme was "Connections," and Kaur's entry resonated with judges precisely because it connected the intimate and the universal: private domestic spaces rendered as shared cultural memory.

## A Punjab Childhood, Rendered in Ink

Kaur's Patiala roots are visible in every panel. The rooftops she draws are unmistakably North Indian — satellite dishes alongside water tanks, washing lines competing with solar panels, the occasional tulsi plant in a corner. But the genius of *Terrace Tales* is that it avoids specificity in favour of archetype. These rooftops belong to Patiala, but they also belong to Lucknow, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, and every Indian city where the terrace functions as an extension of the home.

The wordless format is a deliberate choice. Without text, the book crosses language barriers — a Malayali grandmother and a Punjabi child can both read it. For Kaur, who grew up surrounded by India's visual storytelling traditions (Pahari miniatures, truck art, rangoli), the idea of narrative-through-image came naturally.

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

For NRIs, *Terrace Tales* will trigger something visceral. The Indian rooftop is one of the most powerful nostalgia anchors in the diaspora experience — more evocative than any monument or famous landmark, because it is personal. It is where you flew kites with your cousins, where your mother hung clothes to dry, where your father pointed out constellations on summer nights.

That this memory is now being preserved and celebrated in a prestigious London gallery, by an Indian woman studying in Cambridge, is quietly significant. It joins a growing body of diaspora art — from Jhumpa Lahiri's fiction to Chitra Ganesh's visual work — that treats Indian domestic life not as backdrop but as subject worthy of the highest artistic attention.

The Batsford Prize exhibition at the Batsford Gallery in London will display Kaur's work alongside other 2026 winners and shortlisted entries. For anyone in the UK, it is worth the visit. For everyone else, the work speaks for itself — silently, beautifully, and in a language that every Indian rooftop already knows.

## What Is Next

Kaur is expected to complete her MA later this year. The Batsford Prize often serves as a launchpad for young illustrators entering the publishing industry, and *Terrace Tales* — with its cross-cultural appeal and distinctive format — has clear commercial potential as a published book. Whether it lands with an Indian publisher, a British one, or both, the rooftop will finally get the coffee-table treatment it deserves.
